title: Chapter XV

teacherSummary.text: Collins intends to marry a Bennet daughter and, told Jane is likely engaged, shifts to Elizabeth. In Meryton the girls meet the handsome George Wickham; Darcy and Wickham see each other and change color.

vocabulary.context: Philips’ throwing up the parlour window, and loudly seconding the invitation.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “second”: se- (Latin se-, "apart"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To cause to cease being weary
vocabulary.context: Collins repeated his apologies in quitting the room, and was assured with unwearying civility that they were perfectly needless.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “unweary”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.context: The subjection in which his father had brought him up, had given him originally great humility of manner, but it was now a good deal counteracted by the self-conceit of a weak head, living in retirement, and the consequential feelings of early and unexpected prosperity.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “counteract”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.context: Bingley was the principal spokesman, and Miss Bennet the principal object.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “spokesman”: man (Latin manus, "hand"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: To admit a thing as true
vocabulary.context: In pompous nothings on his side, and civil assents on that of his cousins, their time passed till they entered Meryton.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “assent”: as- (Latin ad, "to") + sent (Latin sentire, "to feel"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A scheme for the distribution of prizes by lot or chance
vocabulary.context: Philips protested that they would have a nice comfortable noisy game of lottery tickets, and a little bit of hot supper afterwards.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “lottery”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A ceasing of discontinuance, as of action, whether termporary or final
vocabulary.context: Bennet, with little cessation, of his house and garden at Hunsford.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “cessation”: cess (Latin cedere, "to go, yield") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Teacher note from a root table; verify in an etymological dictionary.

vocabulary.definition: A small piece of paper, cardboard, or the like, serving as a notice, certificate, or distinguishing token of something
vocabulary.context: Philips protested that they would have a nice comfortable noisy game of lottery tickets, and a little bit of hot supper afterwards.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “ticket”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

vocabulary.definition: A loud calling or crying out
vocabulary.context: Philips was quite awed by such an excess of good breeding; but her contemplation of one stranger was soon put an end to by exclamations and inquiries about the other, of whom, however, she could only tell her nieces what they already knew, that Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “exclamation”: ex- (Latin ex, "out of") + -ation (Latin -atio, "the act or result of"). Root not in our table: have students find it.

vocabulary.definition: To ask for, or seek to obtain, by virtue of authority, right, or supposed right
vocabulary.context: Jones’s shop boy in the street, who had told her that they were not to send any more draughts to Netherfield because the Miss Bennets were come away, when her civility was claimed towards Mr.
vocabulary.source: Webster's Revised Unabridged Dictionary (1913), public domain
vocabulary.etymology: “claim”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin.

context.history: Militia officers were socially attractive but often lacked fortune.

significance: The tense meeting foreshadows a hidden history.
discussionQuestions: What does the reaction of Darcy and Wickham suggest?
Where does characterization appear in this chapter, and what effect does it have? Point to one passage.
How does this chapter connect to the book's larger concern with women's limited choices?

items.prompt: Why did Collins come to Longbourn?
options: To choose a wife among the daughters

items.prompt: Whom does Collins choose after Jane?
What happens when Darcy and Wickham meet?
What first impression does Wickham make?
In the line “Philips’ throwing up the parlour window, and loudly seconding the invitation.”, what does “seconding” most nearly mean?
options: To cause to cease being weary

items.prompt: In the line “Collins repeated his apologies in quitting the room, and was assured with unwearying civility that they were perfectly needless.”, what does “unwearying” most nearly mean?
options: To cause to cease being weary

answerKey.answer: To choose a wife among the daughters
To cause to cease being weary

writingPrompts.label: Middle School
writingPrompts.text: In “Chapter XV,” how does Austen show a charming stranger? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence.

writingPrompts.label: HS Freshman
writingPrompts.text: In Chapter XV, how does Austen develop the idea of a charming stranger? State a clear claim, support it with two or three quotations, and explain how the characterization in the chapter helps build that idea.

writingPrompts.label: HS Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how Chapter XV develops the idea of a charming stranger. Make a precise claim, support it with at least three pieces of textual evidence, and explain how the author's use of characterization and foreshadowing shapes that idea. Address one possible counterclaim.

writingPrompts.label: HS Junior
writingPrompts.text: Analyze how the structure of Chapter XV (where it begins, turns and ends) and its characterization shape the reader's understanding of a charming stranger. Identify one place where the text leaves matters uncertain and explain how that uncertainty adds to its meaning.

writingPrompts.label: HS Senior
writingPrompts.text: Two readers disagree about what Chapter XV suggests about a charming stranger. Lay out two plausible interpretations, weigh the evidence for each (including the chapter's characterization and foreshadowing), and argue for the stronger one in a sustained, well-organized essay.

writingPrompts.label: AP
writingPrompts.text: Write a literary argument in which you analyze how Jane Austen uses characterization in Chapter XV to complicate the reader's understanding of a charming stranger. Develop a defensible thesis, select evidence purposefully, and explain how specific choices of diction and syntax create meaning.

writingPrompts.label: College Freshman
writingPrompts.text: Situate Chapter XV within its historical and literary context and argue how the chapter's treatment of a charming stranger responds to that context. Engage with at least one secondary perspective (a critic, historian or the author's own statements), integrate quotations smoothly, and cite in MLA style.

writingPrompts.label: College Sophomore
writingPrompts.text: Read Chapter XV alongside the conventions of its genre and period. Argue how the chapter's handling of a charming stranger follows or bends those conventions, using the characterization as evidence, and test your reading against one published critic. Document two secondary sources in MLA.

writingPrompts.label: College Junior
writingPrompts.text: Apply a named critical approach (for example formalist, historicist, feminist, psychoanalytic or ecocritical) to Chapter XV and its treatment of a charming stranger. State your method, show what it reveals in the chapter's characterization and foreshadowing, and identify where the text resists it.

writingPrompts.label: College Senior
writingPrompts.text: Develop a research argument that reads Chapter XV as evidence for a larger claim about a charming stranger in Pride and Prejudice. Connect close reading of the chapter to the whole novel, engage at least four scholarly sources, and state precisely where your reading departs from theirs (Chicago style).

writingPrompts.label: Graduate / PhD
writingPrompts.text: Develop an original argument that reads Chapter XV as a hinge in the novel's larger treatment of a charming stranger. Position your reading within a named critical conversation (for example formalist, historicist, psychoanalytic, feminist or postcolonial approaches), account for the textual history where relevant, and articulate the stakes of your intervention for scholarship on Pride and Prejudice.

satQuestions.prompt: As used in the text, what does the word “counteracted” most nearly mean?
options: A small piece of paper, cardboard, or the like, serving as a notice, certificate, or distinguishing token of something
A loud calling or crying out
To ask for, or seek to obtain, by virtue of authority, right, or supposed right

satQuestions.passage: In pompous nothings on his side, and civil assents on that of his cousins, their time passed till they entered Meryton. The attention of the younger ones was then no longer to be gained by him. Their eyes were immediately wandering up in the street in quest of the officers, and nothing less than a very smart bonnet indeed, or a really new muslin in a shop window, could recall them.
satQuestions.prompt: Which choice best states a central concern of “Chapter XV”?

annotationFocus.label: Characterization
annotationFocus.lookFor: what characters say, do and think, and how others react to them
annotationFocus.passage: In pompous nothings on his side, and civil assents on that of his cousins, their time passed till they entered Meryton. The attention of the younger ones was then no longer to be gained by him. Their eyes were immediately wandering up in the street in quest of the officers, and nothing less than a very smart bonnet indeed, or a really new muslin in a shop window, could recall them.

annotationFocus.label: Foreshadowing
annotationFocus.lookFor: hints, warnings or images that point to later events

annotationFocus.label: Irony
annotationFocus.lookFor: gaps between what characters expect or say and what is true

segments.activity: Respond in writing to the bell-ringer, then pair-share.
segments.script: Settle in and write for five minutes: What does the reaction of Darcy and Wickham suggest? No wrong answers yet; we will test these ideas against the text. Two volunteers share, and I note key words on the board.

segments.activity: Introduce 5 key words: pronounce, define from context, then the word's history.
segments.script: Today's words are seconding, unwearying, counteracted, spokesman, assents. For each one we read the sentence, guess from context and then check Webster's. Here is the first: “Philips’ throwing up the parlour window, and loudly seconding the invitation.” Webster's says: Immediately following the first. Now the word history: “second”: se- (Latin se-, "apart"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “unweary”: un- (Old English un-, "not"). Root not in our table: have students find it. “counteract”: no root in our classroom table; have students look it up (Etymonline, OED) and record the language of origin. Add each root to your etymology log.

segments.activity: Present the historical and literary background.
segments.script: Here is what the first readers of Pride and Prejudice would have known. Militia officers were socially attractive but often lacked fortune. Why does this chapter matter? The tense meeting foreshadows a hidden history. Write down one question you want answered.

segments.activity: Teacher models a think-aloud on the anchor passage for characterization.
segments.script: Watch me read this the way a careful reader does. I read a sentence, stop, and ask what the author is doing. When I see characterization, I underline it and write in the margin what effect it has. Here I notice the diction and the sentence rhythm, and I connect them to a charming stranger.

segments.activity: Read the anchor passage aloud together; annotate for Characterization, Foreshadowing, Irony.
segments.script: Now we do it together. I read the first sentence and you track along. Mark every example of characterization. Turn to a partner: what does the author want us to notice? I will collect three ideas and we choose the strongest using evidence.
segments.passage: In pompous nothings on his side, and civil assents on that of his cousins, their time passed till they entered Meryton. The attention of the younger ones was then no longer to be gained by him. Their eyes were immediately wandering up in the street in quest of the officers, and nothing less than a very smart bonnet indeed, or a really new muslin in a shop window, could recall them.

segments.activity: Students annotate a new passage independently in the reader, then begin the writing prompt at their rigor.
segments.script: Your turn. Annotate the next page in the app for Characterization, Foreshadowing, Irony: at least three marks with a margin note each. Then open your writing prompt; your level is already set. Middle-school version: In “Chapter XV,” how does Austen show a charming stranger? Write a paragraph that states your claim, quotes two details from the chapter, and explains how each detail supports your idea. Use the characterization you noticed as one piece of evidence. I will circulate and conference.

segments.activity: Structured discussion (think-pair-share or a short Socratic circle).
segments.script: Let's talk. Our question: How does this chapter connect to first impressions and prejudice? Every claim needs a page reference. Respond to the person before you by agreeing, extending or challenging with evidence.

segments.activity: Chapter quiz in the app, then a one-sentence exit ticket.
segments.script: Take the chapter quiz in the app. Then, in one sentence, tell me what this chapter suggests about a charming stranger, backed by one short quotation.

segments.activity: Summarize the lesson and preview the next reading.
segments.script: Today we saw how characterization shapes a charming stranger. Tonight, read the next chapter and add two words to your etymology log.
